summary.text: 女 is a whole-figure pictograph of a woman, now meaning “woman; female.” Early forms are interpreted as a kneeling or seated figure, with accounts differing on the hands’ position.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts a woman. Early forms are interpreted as a kneeling figure with hands crossed at the chest; some forms are described with an added head stroke interpreted as headwear.

components.text: The whole graph depicts a woman; early forms are interpreted as a kneeling figure, sometimes with a head stroke interpreted as headwear. It is not divided into smaller parts.

history.text: Oracle-bone forms are described as a kneeling woman with hands crossed before the chest; some add a head stroke interpreted as headwear. The kneeling posture becomes less apparent in Spring and Autumn bronze forms, and Warring States forms continue those forms with changed stroke manner. Clerical writing turns the vertical kneeling stroke into a horizontal stroke.

Early accounts report 女 used for 母 in an oracle-bone example, for 汝 in bronze inscriptions, and for 如 in Warring States writing. These reported readings are distinct from changes in the graph’s written form; the available evidence does not establish a dated sequence among these uses.

uncertainties.text: Descriptions differ in details of early forms. One source describes crossed hands and sometimes a head stroke interpreted as headwear; other accounts describe a seated or kneeling figure and differ on the hands. The proposed modern-form reversal and breast interpretation are not confirmed by the inspected paleographic accounts.
Early inscription accounts report uses of 女 beyond “woman,” but the available dates and contexts do not establish whether each is a borrowed spelling for another word or a development in meaning.

senses.text: Early inscription accounts report female-related uses; a later dictionary glosses 女 as “woman.” The cited inscription examples are not precisely dated here, so they document early use without proving the graph’s original meaning or priority among early uses. The ordinary meaning “woman; female” is current.
Early inscription accounts report 女 used for 母, including cited oracle-bone examples. This documents an early use or overlap, but does not establish a semantic development from “woman.”

senses.gloss: reported uses for 毋, 每/悔, 汝, 如, and place names
senses.text: Inscription accounts report 女 used for 毋, 每/悔, 汝, 如, and place names. The evidence does not establish whether these were borrowed spellings for other words or meanings of 女, and it gives no dated sequence among them.

A separate lexical reading is recorded with the meaning “give as a wife.” The supplied historical readings distinguish it from 女 “female,” but do not date this use or establish how the meanings are related.

Present-day definition records list “girl” and “feminine”; a dictionary also lists daughter or unmarried girl. These listed meanings do not establish when they arose or how they developed from “woman.”

limitations.text: The reported uses and dictionary glosses do not establish dated transitions among these meanings, so no semantic-development links are asserted.

Pictograph of a woman. Depicts a stick-figure with breasts sitting or squatting down.
婦人也。象形。王育說。凡女之屬皆从女。

Pictogram (象形): a woman with breasts kneeling or standing. In the modern form, the pictogram is reversed from the Oracle Bone script form, and is "facing" toward the right edge of the character: the enclosed area (bounded on the right side by the downward-curving second stroke of the modern form) is the remnant of the figure's right breast, while the figure's left breast has disappeared.
Graphically cognate to 母 (mǔ, “mother”) and 毋, which has developed similarly, but also includes dots for nipples and has retained both breasts. Compare Egyptian 𓁐.
Similar but unrelated to 卩, in which the person kneeling has unspecified gender.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *naq (“woman”). Compare Tibetan ཉག་མོ (nyag mo, “woman”) (Hill, 2019).
Pronunciation 2 is an exoactive derivation of pronunciation 1 (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.field: 甲金文字形及用法；字形義通解
evidence.text: The database describes 女 in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions as a kneeling woman, with knees and toes on the ground, seated on her heels and hands crossed at the chest. It says later bronze forms gradually lose the seated-on-heels shape through writing simplification. It reports early graph uses for woman/female, mother, 毋 ‘not’, 每/悔, and place names; bronze uses include woman, mother, second-person pronoun (later 汝), and 如 ‘as’. These are reported uses/loans and should not be treated as stages in the graphic evolution of 女.

evidence.source: 常用漢字二百字探源（金真姬）
evidence.field: 女 entry: glyph history and oracle-bone examples
evidence.text: The entry characterizes 女 as a pictograph and summarizes Li Xiaoding and Xu Zhongshu as interpreting it as a kneeling person with hands engaged in an activity. It says the original form had become less recognizable by the Warring States period. It cites oracle-bone examples including 合集14002正 for female, 殷虛文字綴合94 for a reading as 母, and other oracle-bone records for a female ancestor/consort and a female person. The examples support early female-related uses while also documenting early interchange or overlap with 母 in particular contexts.

evidence.field: 女 entry: script-form account, senses and cited examples; scan /home/catalin/hanzi-etymology-books/research-ocr/ziyuan-full/page-1100/source.png
evidence.text: The entry calls 女 pictographic. It describes oracle-bone forms as a woman kneeling with her hands crossed before her chest, and says some forms add a head stroke interpreted as headwear. It describes the kneeling posture as less apparent in Spring and Autumn bronze forms, with Warring States forms following those bronze forms with changed stroke manner; clerical writing turns the vertical kneeling stroke into a horizontal stroke. It gives the core meaning as female, contrasted with 男, and cites a bronze-inscription example and the transmitted 易 for 女 meaning female. It separately reports 女 read as 母 in an oracle-bone example, as 汝 in bronze inscriptions, and as 如 in Warring States writing. The entry also records a distinct nù reading for ‘give a woman in marriage’, citing 國語. These source-reported uses and citations do not by themselves establish a dated semantic development or the dates of each cited inscription.
